hints: Look at the small M+1 peak at m/e = 61 first, it tells you about the number of carbon atoms from the natural abundance of carbon-13.
A 2.2% height compared to the M+ peak points to about two carbons, since each carbon adds roughly 1.1% to M+1.
Now use the fragments to choose between the two-carbon candidates, think what m/e = 17 and m/e = 31 would have to be.
walkthrough:
**Use the M+1 peak to count carbons**

All four options have $M_r = 60$, so start with the peak at $m/e = 61$. This is the isotopic peak due mainly to $^{13}\text{C}$.

Relative intensity rule:
$$\text{number of C} \approx \frac{\text{intensity of M+1}}{1.1}$$

**Calculate the carbon number**

Here intensity of M+1 is 2.2 when M+ is 100.
$$\text{number of C} \approx \frac{2.2}{1.1} \approx 2$$
So the compound contains 2 carbon atoms. This fits $\text{HCOOCH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, but not the $\text{C}_3$ compounds.

**Use absence of m/e = 17 to test for OH**

A fragment at $m/e = 17$ would be $\text{OH}^+$. Alcohols and carboxylic acids readily lose $\text{OH}$.
No peak at 17 strongly suggests there is no $\text{-OH}$ group, which rules out ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$.

**Use the fragment at m/e = 31 to confirm**

$m/e = 31$ fits $\text{CH}_3\text{O}^+$ ($12+3+16 = 31$).
Methyl methanoate, $\text{HCOOCH}_3$, can cleave to give $\text{CH}_3\text{O}^+$ easily, and has 2 carbons and no OH group. This matches all the data perfectly.

options.A: Correct. $\text{HCOOCH}_3$ is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$ with $M_r = 60$. Two carbons give M+1 of about 2.2%, it has no OH group so no peak at 17, and it forms $\text{CH}_3\text{O}^+$ at m/e = 31.
options.B: False. $\text{CH}_3\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5$ is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$ with $M_r = 60$ but it has 3 carbons. Its M+1 would be about 3.3%, not 2.2%.
options.C: False. $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ has the right $M_r$ and 2 carbons, but as a carboxylic acid it contains $\text{-OH}$ and would be expected to show an $\text{OH}^+$ fragment at m/e = 17. It also does not readily give a strong m/e = 31 fragment.
options.D: False. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ has $M_r = 60$ but has 3 carbons, so M+1 should be about 3.3%. As an alcohol it contains $\text{-OH}$ and would be expected to show m/e = 17, which is absent.
